title: Al-Hujurat, whole
tomorrow: why does a stranger come running from the far end of a city?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luqman's counsel to his son, ending on a lowered voice. Today's surah opens on voices too, raised ones, outside someone's door.
screen: `LOWER YOUR VOICE.` → `RAISED VOICES, OUTSIDE A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Some people knock. Some people sit in the driveway and honk. In the scene that names this surah, people stand outside the private rooms of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and call out to him to come out. They don't wait. They don't knock. They shout through the walls. The surah says waiting until he came out to them would have been better for them. That's al-Hujurat, the private rooms. And by its end, this little surah of manners answers a very big question: why are people made different at all?
screen: `KNOCKING, OR HONKING.` → `SHOUTING THROUGH THE WALLS.` → `WHY ARE PEOPLE MADE DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: From that doorway the surah reads like a guide to living with people. Don't raise your voices over the Prophet's. If someone untrustworthy brings you news, "verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them; believers are brothers. Don't mock another group; they may be better than you. Don't call each other by insulting nicknames. Avoid much suspicion, don't spy, don't backbite. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: verse after verse opens O ye who believe. Then, near the end, the address widens to everyone: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." One pair at the root of everybody. Nations and tribes are real, and the verse keeps them; it doesn't erase anyone's people. But it gives them a reason: so that you would know one another. Not rank one another. Not wall each other off. Know. And the only ranking that counts is conduct, which God sees, and we mostly don't. A surah that starts with people shouting through a wall ends with the walls between peoples turned into doors.
screen: `VERIFY THE NEWS.` · `NO MOCKING, NO NICKNAMES.` · `O YE WHO BELIEVE, THEN O MANKIND.` · `TRIBES FOR KNOWING, NOT RANKING.` · then, large: `KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person you mostly know by a label: the new kid, the neighbor from somewhere else, the coworker with the accent. For the sit, just hold them there, and find one real question you'd like to ask them.
Al-Hujurat. The private rooms: surah 49, the surah of manners, which ends by turning nations and tribes into a reason to meet.
Keep this one close: know one another, not rank, not wall off, but know. Day done, door open.

howItsDone: Al-Hujurat 49:13 is quoted by Muslims in sermons and talks about the equal dignity of people of every nation; the surah's rules on verifying news, nicknames and backbiting are taught as everyday manners.

fork.setup: at the senior picnic, everyone sits with their own group again. a friend wants to mix up the tables. what fits 49:13?
options: leave it: the verse says God made tribes, so stay with yours.
mix them, and tell everyone their backgrounds don't matter at all.

fork.reveal: the verse keeps nations and tribes, and gives them a purpose: that ye may know one another. not walls, and not erasing anyone.

original.note: Arabic: the private rooms. surah 49 takes its name from the scene at the Prophet's door.

chat.says: dad explained: bilal's family just moved from cairo, he needed work. i've never asked bilal one thing about himself
options: Start there. Tribes exist 'that ye may know one another.' Ask him something real.
Leave it. He's from a different background, and the verse says stick to your tribe.
Skip the questions. The verse says backgrounds don't matter, so treat him like anyone.
chat.meaning: 49:13 keeps nations and tribes and gives them a reason: that ye may know one another. Knowing someone starts with asking.

The occasion (a delegation, in tafsir) is not named. Confirm.
'Verse after verse opens O ye who believe' refers to 49:1, 2, 6, 11, 12; 49:13 opens 'O mankind'. No count is given. Confirm.

Unity thread (user request: one human race): 49:13 taught in the Qur'an's own words: one pair at the root of everyone, nations and tribes kept, not erased, given the purpose of knowing one another, and nobility by conduct.
